text.p: Australian farmers face a grim six months, with incomes again declining as commodity prices fall and world demand slumps, the government's chief forecasting agency said on Tuesday.

In contrast, miners are set to see exports grow in the next 18 months, fuelled by world economic and industrial growth, the Australian Bureau of Agricutural and Resource Economics (ABARE) told a commodities conference.
"Lower prices for farm commodities are expected to result in reduced farm profitability this financial year," said ABARE executive director Brian Fisher.
Fisher said the overall value of Australia's commodity exports will rise 1.8 percent to A$58.5 billion (US$44.6 billion) in the year to June 30, 1997 and a further seven percent in 1997/98.
But farmers were cautioned to brace for lower profits, despite a return to good growing weather across most of Australia after years of drought.
While miners are poised to benefit from a resurgence in international minerals prices, the farming sector is still carrying the weight of depressed markets, Fisher said.
Farm exports are forecast to be worth A$20 billion in 1996/97, one percent less than the previous year, with no growth expected in 1997/98, he said.
John Anderson, the minister for primary industries and energy, said circumstances could drive some farmers to ruin.
The value of wheat exports is forecast to fall by 10 percent to A$3.0 billion in 1996/97, reflecting low international prices amid a bumper Australian harvest.
Sugar exports are suffering from weak world prices and values of wool and beef exports are also depressed.

"Some farmers will not remain on the land," Anderson told the conference. "The impact over the last decade of poor prices, terrible seasons and sustained high real interest rates is simply unrecoverable for some farmers."
Two bright spots are dairy products and cotton, where export earnings are seen rising over the next two fiscal years.
On the other hand, ABARE sees the value of mineral exports improving slightly to around A$36 billion this year and exceeding A$38 billion next year, Fisher said.
Aluminium prices should increase 11 percent in 1996/97 and iron ore prices are also on the rise, he said.
Gold prices are forecast to average US$375 an ounce in calendar 1997, down three percent from 1996, but well above current market prices of under US$350.
Australian gold production should reach a record 303 tonnes in 1996/97, maintaining its ranking as the world's third largest producer, ABARE gold analyst Simon Middleton said.
"Gold mining companies have been very active," he said.
